sources.news_title: Trump’s Exercise Cut Risks Turning South Korea-US Alliance Readiness Into a Bargaining Chip
sources.text:
Hours before South Korea and the United States began Ulchi Freedom Shield on August 17, U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the exercise. He called the drills “costly” and an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea, emphasized his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, and linked his displeasure to Seoul’s refusal to join U.S. action against Iran. He noted in a post on Truth Social that the exercises were being scaled back, not scrapped entirely, only because “it is too late to cancel.”
The exercise nevertheless started as scheduled, while the Pentagon offered no public explanation of what would be cut. This ambiguity makes the immediate military consequences difficult to measure. It also reveals a more serious alliance problem. A recurring combined exercise, developed through months of bilateral planning against a nuclear-armed adversary, was recast overnight as an instrument of presidential diplomacy and leverage over an ally.
One shortened exercise – if indeed Ulchi Freedom Shield is scaled back – will not undo the South Korea-U.S. combined defense posture. Repeated uncertainty over whether future exercises will proceed, however, could weaken readiness, disrupt the transition of wartime operational control, and reduce confidence in alliance consultation. If Washington wants to use military restraint to reopen diplomacy with Pyongyang, it must do so in concert with Seoul and in return for meaningful North Korean restraint.
The Last-Minute Reduction
Ulchi Freedom Shield is an 11-day combined exercise involving about 18,000 South Korean personnel. It integrates computer-assisted command-post training with field exercises and this year incorporates lessons from recent wars, including drone operations, GPS disruption, and cyberattacks. Even before Trump’s order, the allies had planned 14 battalion-level or larger field exercises, down from 17 in 2025. The overall number of South Korean participants remained roughly unchanged.
Because the order – if a post on Truth Social can be called that – arrived only hours before the exercise began, canceling or redesigning the command-post phase would create more disruption than savings. The likelier near-term options are narrower U.S. participation, fewer supporting assets, or reductions in field events that have not yet occurred. Until detailed guidance emerges, it’s difficult to evaluate the actual impact.
However, the value of Ulchi Freedom Shield cannot be counted only in troops or field events. It rehearses the machinery that would allow two national militaries to operate as one force in a crisis: command relationships, intelligence flows, reinforcement, logistics, missile defense, and civil-military coordination. Smaller training can mitigate gaps, but it cannot fully reproduce theater-level decision-making under pressure.
Ulchi Freedom Shield 2026 also has an unusually important institutional purpose. The allies planned to use it to assess agreed capabilities and systems supporting the conditions-based transition of wartime operational control. Seoul hoped that a successful assessment would permit certification of the future Combined Forces Command’s full operational capability and support discussion of a transition timeline later this year. A major last-minute change could therefore affect more than readiness; it could complicate an alliance project that Washington itself has long encouraged.
This exposes a contradiction in current U.S. policy. The 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy calls for South Korea to take primary responsibility for deterring North Korea with “critical but more limited” U.S. support. That shift requires stronger combined planning and credible validation of South Korean command capacity. Exercises are one of the main mechanisms for transferring and testing greater responsibility. Curtailing them, especially without prior discussion, makes burden-sharing harder to implement, even as Washington demands more of it.
Trump’s reference to Iran is even more damaging. He ended his post with a comment criticizing Seoul’s reluctance to join the Israeli-U.S. strikes on Iran. Trump himself called the Iran factor “somewhat unrelated (?)” (sic) to the decision to scale back exercises, only adding to the confusion.
The U.S.-ROK Mutual Defense Treaty is centered on “common danger” in “the Pacific area.” Any South Korean contribution to operations involving Iran must also account for domestic legal procedures, available forces, and immediate requirements on the peninsula.
Washington can ask Seoul to contribute to wider security challenges, and South Korea should seriously consider requests involving shared interests such as maritime security and the protection of sea lanes. But conditioning joint exercises – a core mechanism of peninsula defense – on participation in an unrelated military campaign changes calls into question alliance solidarity.
Seoul is increasing defense spending, expanding conventional capabilities, and accepting a larger role in deterring North Korea – all in line with Trump’s stated preferences. A demand for allies to take greater responsibility for their own defense is sustainable when paired with reliable U.S. support and predictable consultation. If U.S. participation can be reduced suddenly because Seoul declined an out-of-area request, South Korean policymakers will reasonably question whether alliance decisions are still governed by common strategy.
The Risk of Seoul Being Sidelined
Trump has done this before. After the 2018 Singapore summit with Kim Jong Un, Trump surprised both South Korean and U.S. military officials by announcing the suspension of major exercises. The pause created space for diplomacy with North Korea, but it also produced a measurable degradation in combined-force readiness. Three Trump-Kim meetings ultimately had no lasting impact on curtailing North Korea’s nuclear weapons or ballistic missile development.
Certainly military restraint can support diplomacy when it is coordinated, limited in time, and exchanged for reciprocal measures. The 2018 experience, however, shows the danger of granting a visible concession before North Korea agrees to make any concessions of its own.
Trump may hope that a reduction in Ulchi Freedom Shield will help revive direct dialogue with Kim. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung also favors renewed engagement, and the presidential office responded cautiously by expressing hope that the “friendly” Kim-Trump relationship “will lead to meaningful US-North Korea dialogue.” A coordinated reduction could therefore support both governments’ diplomatic objectives.
The current strategic setting, however, is less favorable than it was in 2018. North Korea has deepened military cooperation with Russia. North Korean troops have gained battlefield experience in the Russia-Ukraine war, while Pyongyang continues to improve its missiles and has conducted two ballistic missile launches since August 6. Just before Ulchi Freedom Shield, North Korea threatened to strengthen its nuclear deterrent in response to the exercise. Trump just rewarded this behavior, even calling North Korea’s behavior in general “unthreatening and respectful.”
Meanwhile, Pyongyang has recast inter-Korean relations through its “two hostile states” policy and consistently rejects all outreach from Seoul. Under these conditions, a U.S. concession made without prior allied agreement can reinforce Pyongyang’s preference for dealing directly with Washington while excluding Seoul. This is the dynamic South Koreans often call “Korea passing.” It is not an inevitable result of North Korea-U.S. diplomacy, but the risk grows when Washington demonstrates that it can alter combined military activity first and consult Seoul afterward.
Restoring Joint Control of Alliance Decisions
Seoul should avoid both a public confrontation with Trump and passive acceptance of an undefined order. The immediate priority is a joint political and military review that clarifies which activities are affected and protects the essential command-post functions, the operational control assessment, and training involving critical U.S. enablers. If some field events or U.S. deployments are reduced, the allies should identify compensatory training rather than allow temporary cuts to become an unplanned new baseline.
The two governments also need rules for future exercise adjustments. Any change intended to advance diplomacy should be jointly decided, time-limited, reversible, and linked to observable North Korean action. Exercise policy should remain separate from trade disputes and requests for South Korean participation in operations outside the peninsula. Washington may seek wider contributions from Seoul, but those discussions belong in their own strategic and legal framework.
For its part, South Korea should continue strengthening independent intelligence, command-and-control, missile defense, precision-strike, and sustainment capabilities. Greater self-reliance will make the alliance more resilient to changes in U.S. force posture. It cannot substitute for combined training, however, because deterrence depends on an adversary believing that U.S. and South Korean forces can fight together, not merely that each possesses capable weapons.
The alliance can absorb one late and partially implemented order. It will struggle if combined readiness becomes a bargaining chip that can be exchanged for diplomatic atmospherics or used to punish disagreement on unrelated issues. Trump’s decision could still become the opening to a coordinated diplomatic initiative. Without reciprocal North Korean steps and genuine consultation with Seoul, however, it is more likely to expose a widening gap between the alliance’s formal commitments and the way its most consequential decisions are made.

Trump Cuts US-South Korea Drills, Citing Good Ties With North Korea’s Leader Despite Christian Persecution (Worthy News In-Depth)
by Stefan J. Bos, Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief
WASHINGTON/PYONGYANG (Worthy News) – U.S. President Donald J. Trump announced Sunday that he had ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” military exercises with key regional ally South Korea, citing his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Seoul’s refusal to assist Washington in its confrontation with Iran.
The move underscored Trump’s renewed emphasis on personal diplomacy with Kim despite longstanding concerns about North Korea’s human rights record, including the plight of Christians and other religious believers under the communist government.
“Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
“These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful,” he added.
MAJOR MILITARY DRILLS
Trump said it was too late to cancel the exercises entirely and that he had therefore instructed Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to “substantially reduce” them.
The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, scheduled for August 17-27, involve about 18,000 South Korean troops and are intended to strengthen readiness against threats from nuclear-armed North Korea.
This year’s exercises were expected to include operations aimed at countering drones, GPS interference and cyberattacks as Washington and Seoul adapt to North Korea’s evolving military capabilities.
Pyongyang has repeatedly condemned the exercises as rehearsals for an invasion and warned last week of strong countermeasures. North Korea also recently fired ballistic missiles toward the sea ahead of the drills.
IRAN DISPUTE
U.S. and South Korean officials have defended the exercises as defensive and crucial for maintaining the readiness of their decades-old alliance, particularly as North Korea continues developing nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles.
Trump also linked his decision to Seoul’s refusal to participate in U.S. actions involving Iran.
“While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks!’” Trump wrote.
“Therefore, and based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!” the president added.
SOUTH KOREAN PEACE OFFER
The decision came shortly after South Korean President Lee Jae Myung extended another diplomatic overture toward North Korea, calling for talks aimed at replacing the armistice that halted the 1950-53 Korean War with a permanent peace arrangement.
Because the conflict ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty, North and South Korea technically remain at war more than seven decades later.
Lee has advocated peaceful coexistence and renewed dialogue, including efforts to reduce military tensions and address North Korea’s nuclear weapons program.
Yet Kim has not extended a similar olive branch. His government has rejected Seoul’s dialogue overtures, increasingly portrayed South Korea as a hostile state and strengthened military cooperation with Russia.
RUSSIA MILITARY TIES
North Korea has provided troops and weapons to support Moscow’s war against Ukraine, giving its forces battlefield experience that U.S. and South Korean military officials have warned could further improve Pyongyang’s military capabilities.
Trump’s description of North Korea as “unthreatening and respectful” also comes despite longstanding international concerns about the Kim government’s human rights record, including its treatment of Christians.
Christian advocacy group Open Doors ranks North Korea as the world’s most dangerous country in which to be a Christian on its 2026 World Watch List.
Open Doors says Christians discovered practicing their faith can face imprisonment in notorious labor camps or execution, with relatives also potentially facing punishment.
CHRISTIANS UNDERGROUND
Christianity is viewed as particularly threatening by the communist government because loyalty to God challenges the personality cult surrounding the ruling Kim family, Christian rights investigators say.
Despite the dangers, an underground Christian community continues to worship secretly, reportedly relying on whispered prayers, memorized Scripture and clandestine gatherings among trusted relatives and friends.
North Korea’s 2020 “anti-reactionary thought” legislation further strengthened restrictions on outside cultural and religious influences, while possession of a Bible can result in severe punishment, according to Christian rights investigators.
American evangelist Franklin Graham has nevertheless expressed hope over the years that engagement between Washington and Pyongyang could eventually improve conditions for Christians.
GRAHAM FAMILY HISTORY
His family has an unusual history with North Korea. His father, evangelist Billy Graham, visited the country in 1992 and 1994 and met North Korea’s founding leader Kim Il Sung.
Billy Graham also addressed students and faculty at Kim Il Sung University and spoke publicly about the Christian faith during a period when few prominent Western religious leaders had access to the isolated communist nation.
His wife, Ruth Bell Graham, who attended school in Pyongyang during the 1930s, returned in 1997 and spoke at the capital’s Bongsu Church, telling worshippers: “I pray that each one of you will know, as I discovered during my school days here, that God so loved you, that he gave his only begotten Son, that if you would believe in him, you will not perish, but will have everlasting life.”
Franklin Graham later made several humanitarian visits to North Korea through the Christian relief organization Samaritan’s Purse and urged Trump during his earlier presidency to pursue engagement with Pyongyang.
TRUMP RAISED CHRISTIANS
Trump has said he personally raised the persecution of Christians with Kim while discussing nuclear weapons and other issues during their historic diplomacy.
Following their first summit in Singapore in June 2018, Trump was specifically asked whether he had raised the plight of Christians with the North Korean leader.
“I brought it up, absolutely,” Trump responded, before adding: “Christians, yes, we brought it up very strongly.”
Trump also referred to Franklin Graham’s longstanding involvement with North Korea, saying Graham had the issue “very close to his heart” and adding: “It did come up, and things will be happening.”
LITTLE CHANGE REPORTED
Yet nearly eight years later, there is little evidence that Kim’s government has fulfilled those expectations.
The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom has said religious freedom remains virtually nonexistent in North Korea, where Christians and other religious believers can face severe punishment for practicing their faith.
Trump’s decision to scale back the military exercises could therefore become an early test of whether his personal diplomacy with Kim can reopen stalled negotiations over North Korea’s nuclear weapons, reduce tensions on the Korean Peninsula and improve the plight of persecuted Christians—or whether Pyongyang will accept the military concession without offering comparable steps toward peace.

sources.news_title: Trump reduces US-South Korea drills, citing lack of help on Iran
sources.text:
Trump reduces US-South Korea drills, citing lack of help on Iran
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump told the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” joint military exercises with South Korea and indicated his decision to do so was driven by frustration the longtime U.S. ally hadn’t provided more support for his war with Iran.
Trump said in a social post Sunday the drills were costly and sent an “inappropriate signal” to North Korea, citing his “very good relationship” with its leader Kim Jong Un. A 10-day joint exercise involving some 18,000 South Korean troops was scheduled to begin Monday with the goal of addressing new threats from North Korea, officials in Seoul said last week.
Trump’s announcement appeared to catch Seoul by surprise. South Korea’s Defense Ministry said on Monday the drills would continue as planned, but later President Lee Jae Myung’s office said that Seoul and Washington would coordinate closely on the details. Seoul is also in close consultations with Washington on ways to make “practical and military contributions” on the Middle East issues, the office said in a statement.
South Korea, like many U.S. allies, has declined to get involved in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, which began with airstrikes on Feb. 28. Trump has previously complained about European allies refusing to let the U.S. use their airfields to launch attacks.
In his social post, Trump said South Korea had declined to “join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran.” He said that while it was too late to cancel the exercises, they would be reduced.
Trump’s apparent decision to again use a military commitment as leverage may cause concern among other Asia-Pacific allies such as Japan and Australia. Both have security treaties with the U.S., but have also opted to stay out of the Iran conflict.
“Japan will certainly be concerned,” said Adam Farrar, a senior geoeconomics analyst at Bloomberg Economics and former director on the U.S. National Security Council covering Korea in both the Trump and Biden administrations. “If this was driven by Iran, they themselves are at risk, given their own unwillingness to get involved.”
“No matter what the reason is, this type of last-minute decision will raise questions about the U.S. commitment to its Asian allies and potentially impact deterrence,” Farrar added.
Japan’s Foreign Ministry didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump’s announcement came as the lone U.S. aircraft carrier in the Asia-Pacific region, the USS George Washington, was being diverted from the region to the Middle East, according to the U.S. Naval Institute. The U.S. typically keeps at least one carrier in the region to help deter China and North Korea.
The decision by Trump may also be driven by other points of tension in the relationship. It comes following a media report that Washington is pressing Seoul to accelerate plans for strategic investment projects in the U.S.
South Korea has made less visible progress on fleshing out the strategic projects that form part of a $350 billion investment pledge than Japan has with a similar $550 billion commitment. Both countries made the investment pledges during trade negotiations with the U.S. to limit tariffs on their export-dependent economies.
There is a precedent for Trump scaling back joint exercises. While the U.S. and South Korea have conducted joint military drills for decades, they were curtailed during Trump’s first presidency when he negotiated with Kim. Those talks collapsed without any agreement on North Korea’s nuclear weapons program.
“This time, the rationale is less clear. With Russian backing, Kim is in a stronger position and has so far shown little interest in engagement,” Farrar said.
Trump’s announcement raises the question of how the exercises, known as Ulchi Freedom Shield, might be reduced at short notice. U.S. military officials have portrayed the drills as a means to counter North Korean capabilities that have been honed on the battlefield, as Pyongyang continues to provide military support for Russia in its war on Ukraine.
As well as testing ballistic missile systems, North Korea has gained exposure to modern technology such as drones.
North Korea has made its displeasure at the drills clear. On Wednesday it fired a ballistic missile off its east coast, six days after launching a short-range ballistic missile. On Friday it vowed to continue exercising its right to self-defense.
“It is our consistent principle of ensuring security to respond to a new level of a threat with a new level of a deterrent,” a spokesperson for North Korea’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency.
Despite ongoing friction, South Korean President Lee on Saturday called for dialogue with North Korea and pledged to take steps to reduce military tensions and establish peaceful coexistence on the peninsula in a Liberation Day address. South Korea will fulfill its role as a “peacemaker” and stakeholder in stable relations on the Korean peninsula, Lee said.
On Monday, Lee’s office responded positively to Trump’s comments about Kim. In its statement it said it expects the friendly relations between the leaders of the U.S. and North Korea would lead to “meaningful” dialogue for peace on the Korean peninsula.
China said it would welcome renewed dialogue between the U.S. and North Korea following Trump’s social post. “We have noticed relevant reports. Maintaining peace and stability in the peninsula and promoting the political solution of the peninsula issue fits the interest of all sides,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian said at a regular press briefing.
The Iran war has sharply increased the price of oil and gas and put pressure on Trump’s Republican party heading into midterm elections. The U.S. has said it is readying economic measures against Tehran, in an effort to force Iran to capitulate after months of stalled talks.
Nonetheless, North Korea “remains unfinished business for Trump, who clearly wants another go at direct diplomacy with Kim,” said Jeremy Chan, a senior analyst for China and Northeast Asia at the Eurasia Group.
“However, the fundamental obstacle to resumed diplomacy remains Trump’s unwillingness to acknowledge North Korea’s nuclear weapons program,” he said.

sources.news_title: Trump burns allies over Iran. South Korea and Oman are next.
sources.text:
President Trump spent the weekend turning on two US security partners. He ordered a cutback in joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his “very good relationship” with Kim Jong Un, the North Korean dictator — and threatened to bomb Oman, one of the countries mediating between Washington and Tehran.
On Sunday, Trump posted on Truth Social that based on his “very good relationship with Kim Jong Un” and the finances required, he ordered Pete Hegseth to “substantially reduce” annual joint military exercises with South Korea, designed to prepare against threats from North Korea. At the end of his post: “While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, “No thanks!”
And on Monday afternoon, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office a similar account of his conversation with South Korea President Lee Jae Myung on Iran. “We can’t go around and protect all of these countries, especially when they’re not there to help us,” Trump said.
Seoul is downplaying it. South Korea’s Defense Ministry said the exercises began Monday as planned, and President Lee Jae Myung said the two governments had “maintained close coordination” on joint training and would keep doing so.
But the reversal is abrupt. Just three months ago, as the Associated Press noted, Hegseth praised South Korea for raising defense spending and “assuming primary responsibility for the security of the Korean Peninsula” — a shift he called proof of “alliance burden-sharing that all of America’s partners would do well to follow.” It’s the same pattern the administration ran on NATO members who declined to back the war on Iran.
Regarding Oman, Trump told Fox News on Monday that “if Oman gets in the way [of US-Iran negotiations], we’ll bomb the shit out of them.” Oman is reportedly close to an agreement with Iran to restore commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the passageway that carried 20 percent of the world’s crude oil before the US and Israeli strikes on Iran began in February.
Oman is also a strategic partner of the US in the region and often acts as a diplomatic mediator between the US and Iran. The US holds a security agreement with Oman that allows it to access Omani airfield and port facilities for military purposes.
It looks like yet another time where Trump makes decisions built on personal squabbles rather than its critical security relationships.

sources.news_title: Trump’s Break with South Korea Projects Weakness in the Pacific
sources.text:
Confusing adversaries and allies is a basic foreign policy mistake. Leveraging enemies to attack friends is a deeper failure. President Trump committed both errors on Sunday when he announced that he was ordering the Pentagon to “substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises” with South Korea. According to his post on social media, the president’s justifications were his “very good relationship” with Pyongyang’s dictator Kim Jong-un, and Seoul’s failure to help Washington in its war with Tehran.
Trump’s explanation contradicts his dismissal of Seoul five months ago: “WE NEVER DID” need South Korea’s help to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Nor did America, in Trump’s telling, need anyone’s help. Now, months later, the president is revisiting a gambit he played in his first term: scaling down joint exercises with Seoul, apparently as an olive branch to Kim.
Trump may have legitimate reasons to be frustrated with South Korea. The liberal party in Seoul has an established track record of engagement with China, and has actively sought to weaken American sanctions on North Korea in years past. We should expect allies to act as allies.
It is equally true that America’s partners should expect the global hegemony to act predictably in its own interests. Regardless of Seoul’s behavior, Washington benefits when Pyongyang is hemmed in and deterred from adventurism and belligerence. More broadly, America’s interests demand that North Korea never unify the peninsula. For these reasons alone, military exercises with South Korea should persist.
Trump’s idiosyncratic view of international relations risks unwittingly empowering America’s enemies. To be sure, Kim is delighted by any indication of American weakness, and will move to exploit any daylight between Washington and Seoul. Of greater import is how Pyongyang’s northern neighbor views this move.
Xi Jinping has had ample opportunity to take the measure of Donald Trump. His first interaction with the president in 2017 consisted of Trump temporarily leaving the dining hall in Mar-a-Lago to order a strike on Syria. Trump’s choreographed bravado signaled strength and resolve to Xi, as did the president’s successful operation against Nicholas Maduro in his second term.
But Xi has also witnessed Trump’s fundamental rejection of traditional categories for America’s friends and enemies. Trump has accused Volodymyr Zelensky of starting the war with Russia. He heard Trump scold Taiwan earlier this year as he left Beijing, insisting that Taipei lower the temperature with China. He also took note of Trump’s delay of arms sales to Taiwan. And, of course, the whole world witnessed Trump’s repeated attempts last year to downgrade America’s alliance with South Korea.
Confusing allies and adversaries risks misallocating trust and threats, like a chef mistaking sugar for salt. Trump needs to maintain deterrence in East Asia. Two wars are already raging in Eastern Europe and the Middle East. In response to the latter, the Pentagon recently redeployed the USS George Washington from the Indo-Pacific to the Persian Gulf to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln. No carriers are now in or near East Asia. Compounding this capability shortfall is the drawdown of Tomahawk missiles and other standoff platforms the Pentagon would need in a China scenario. Trump is coupling a numbers problem with a judgment problem.
These intersecting trends present Xi, and any other anti-American despot, with an easy response: follow Kim’s lead. Convince Trump that you’re “unthreatening and respectful,” and reap the windfall of unilateral concessions from America. As a bonus, the administration in Washington may blame America’s allies for being “hostile.” Trump already fell into these patterns with Taiwan earlier this summer. Xi will likely seek to pull the president further down this road.
To a point, the president’s frustrations with allies are understandable. More than any of his predecessors, Trump has called on America’s partners to do their part and contribute to their own security. For that, he deserves great credit. But nixing readiness exercises on the Korean Peninsula, with nuclear table stakes, smacks of poor judgment and misplaced optimism in the president’s own ability to untangle intractable challenges that go back to 1950. Ignoring the historical roots of the present is a quick ticket to catastrophe. The challenge of North Korea isn’t the lack of dealmaking presidents or petulant partners in Seoul, but Pyongyang’s Communist ideology, Washington’s failure to prevent its nuclearization, and haphazard policies that have oscillated from confrontation to conciliation.
Trump is unknowingly playing into that perverse pattern. By doing so, he is projecting weakness to Kim Jong-un’s northern neighbor and East Asia’s most powerful dictator. Canceling military exercises with South Korea is likely unfinished business from Trump’s first term. The day may come when the president sees the wisdom of his former advisors who counseled against doing so.

Trump betrays South Korea for his pen pal Kim Jong Un
sources.text:
President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that he planned to retreat from America’s longtime alliance with South Korea, adding that nation to the growing list of American allies that he has insulted and even endangered in his second term.
On his social media account Trump praised his “very good relationship” with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un and said that he was ordering the U.S. military to “substantially reduce” involvement in upcoming joint military exercises with South Korea.
Trump said the exercises with South Korea were “totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea, a nation that has been “unthreatening and respectful” while Trump has been president.
The broadside against South Korea runs counter to more than 70 years of close relations between the two countries, which has endured since the end of the Korean War. Since being sworn in in January 2025, Trump has been involved in hostile exchanges with countries like Canada, Mexico, and the United Kingdom, among others, sowing international discord after decades of strong ties.
Trump’s praise of North Korea not only causes international problems, but it undermines his rhetoric on domestic politics. North Korea is one of the world’s most prominent communist nations, yet Trump has been (inaccurately) decrying the Democratic Party for purported communist influence. By giving in to Kim, Trump gives communism more of an influence over world affairs than it has had in decades.
Since his first term Trump has heaped praise on Kim despite—or perhaps because of—the authoritarian government in North Korea that has made it a global pariah for decades. North Korea is a closed off military dictatorship where individual rights are suppressed and dedication to the whims and desires of the Kim family’s generational dictatorship have even contributed to mass starvation.
Trump gave North Korea a public relations coup in 2019 by meeting for a photo shoot with Kim in the demilitarized zone, even saluting a North Korean military officer. The two leaders have exchanged laudatory letters with each other and Trump said “we fell in love.”

Trump also cited South Korea declining deeper involvement in his military strikes against Iran as another reason for retreat. Trump’s decision has caused global chaos, particularly because the strikes pushed Iran to reduce traffic along the Strait of Hormuz, thus reducing global fuel supply. South Korea is extremely reliant on that fuel and the Iran war has triggered severe economic problems within that nation.
Trump has made it clear that he has an affinity for dictatorship and has tried to lead America as if he is an unquestioned autocrat (aided by a compliant Republican Party). U.S. ally South Korea has long faced threats from North Korea.
President Donald Trump announced Sunday that had directed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to "substantially reduce" joint U.S.-South Korean military exercises, citing his "very good" relationship with North Korea's Supreme Leader Kim Jong Un.
"Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea," Trump wrote on his social media platform.

In 2006, North Korea tested its first nuclear weapon and has since been expanding its atomic weapons stockpile -- despite international condemnation and sanctions led by successive U.S. administrations -- alongside a ballistic missile research program which has produced munitions capable of reaching the continental U.S.

sources.news_title: Trump Orders Major Cut To U.S.-South Korea Military Drills Over Cost And Kim Ties
sources.text:
President Donald Trump directed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Sunday to substantially reduce the annual joint military exercises with South Korea, known as Ulchi Freedom Shield, which began Monday as scheduled.
Trump cited the cost of the drills, paid largely by the United States, and said they send an inappropriate and hostile signal to North Korea, with which he said he maintains a very good relationship.
The announcement came hours before the 11-day exercises were set to start. South Korean military authorities confirmed the drills are proceeding as previously notified and scheduled, according to The Korea Herald.
Trump’s Statement on Truth Social
In a Truth Social post Sunday, Trump wrote the following:
Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea. These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful. Therefore, and based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises! While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, “No thanks!” Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP
The Pentagon did not immediately specify details of the reduction. A Pentagon spokesperson referred questions to the White House.
Details of the Exercises
Freedom Shield is an annual series of defensive exercises involving approximately 18,000 South Korean troops and a portion of the 28,500 U.S. troops stationed in South Korea. The drills, scheduled to run through August 27, focus on readiness against North Korean threats and this year include training to counter drones, GPS disruption, and cyberattacks, Military.com reported.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff confirmed the exercises began Monday. Personnel from United Nations Command member states were also expected to participate.
South Korean Response
South Korean officials said the exercises would proceed as planned. Seoul stated it was reviewing Trump’s comments and expressed hope that improved relations between Washington and Pyongyang could lead to meaningful talks, according to BBC News.
North Korea has not issued an immediate public response. The regime has historically denounced the joint exercises as rehearsals for invasion.
Background on the Alliance
The United States and South Korea have conducted joint military exercises for more than 70 years. About 28,500 American troops remain stationed in South Korea under the longstanding alliance.
Trump’s order marks the first time in his current term that he has directed a scaling back of the drills with South Korea.

sources.news_title: Trump’s South Korea Shift Tests a Key U.S. Alliance
sources.text:
On the eve of the 10-day Ulchi Freedom Shield military drills —involving 18,000 South Korean troops alongside thousands of U.S. and U.N. forces—President Donald Trump dropped one of his trademark bombshells. Announcing he would “substantially reduce” American participation, Trump cited his “very good relationship with Kim Jong Un” and need to rebuke Seoul for refusing to join his war against Iran.
“These exercises are not only costly … but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile to a country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been president, has been unthreatening and respectful,” Trump posted on Truth Social.
In response, South Korea’s presidential Blue House said it remained in “close coordination" with Washington regarding the drills, which had begun as “previously notified and scheduled,” according to its defence ministry.
Still, the decision deals a severe blow to American alliance credibility. Reducing participation in exercises underpinning a 72-year mutual defense treaty with democratic South Korea, while Trump emphasizes his personal relationship with Kim, raises questions about the durability of U.S. security commitments in the Asia-Pacific. At the same time, it whitewashes a police state ranked 3/100 by rights group Freedom House—a regime whose sole formal treaty allies are primary U.S. adversaries China and Russia.
Furthermore, Trump’s assertion that Pyongyang has been “unthreatening and respectful” stands in contrast with North Korea’s continued military activity. Since Trump re-entered office, North Korea has conducted 24 ballistic missile tests—alongside numerous cruise missile and air-defense firings—including a launch just last Wednesday.
Pyongyang has also aggressively expanded its global military footprint following its June 2024 comprehensive strategic partnership with Moscow, dispatching more than 14,000 North Korean troops, artillery ammunition, and ballistic missiles to support Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine. (Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Kim is preparing to deploy 30,000 more.)
Trump’s criticism of South Korea for declining to help “denuclearize” Iran also sits uneasily alongside North Korea’s longstanding role in the development of Tehran’s strategic weapons programs. From a counter-proliferation perspective, North Korea presents a distinct challenge: unlike Iran, it already possesses an operational nuclear arsenal and has an extensive history of transferring missile and military technology abroad.
“The North Koreans provided Iran with technical assistance, building turnkey factories, technology design, production capabilities, tactics—those kinds of things,” says Daniel Pinkston, an international relations expert at Troy University in Seoul. “Technological agreements and high-level scientific visits go back years.”
During the 1980–1988 Iran–Iraq War, North Korea emerged as one of Tehran’s primary arms suppliers. That relationship deepened following the collapse of Soviet subsidies in the early 1990s, when Pyongyang bartered missile technology for Iranian crude oil to keep its depleted economy afloat.
Tehran purchased North Korean Scud-B and Scud-C missiles, using them as the blueprints for its own Shahab-1 and Shahab-2 ballistic missile programs. Later, North Korea’s Nodong-1 missile was adapted into the Shahab-3—the backbone of Iran’s modern long-range strike capabilities, including variants like the Emad and Ghadr. Declassified intelligence indicates Iran specifically modified the nose cones of its Shahab-3 missiles to accommodate miniaturized nuclear warheads.
North Korean military engineers—renowned for building massive subterranean installations—also helped Iran design and construct hardened missile silos, underground networks, and nuclear facility bunkers. Beyond missile architecture, Pyongyang supplied Iran with midget submarines, anti-ship missiles, rocket launchers, and specialized commando training.
While Western intelligence agencies have debated periodic reports of Iranian scientists attending North Korean nuclear tests, Pyongyang’s willingness to proliferate nuclear infrastructure elsewhere is beyond doubt. In 2007, an Israeli airstrike destroyed Syria’s covert Al-Kibar facility—a plutonium-producing reactor built by North Korea that was a carbon copy of its 5-megawatt reactor at Yongbyon.
Beyond diplomacy, scaling back joint drills carries immediate tactical consequences. South Korean and U.S. military commanders had planned to use the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises to adapt to evolving battlefield tactics showcased by North Korean forces in Ukraine, including drone swarm integration, electronic GPS jamming, and coordinated cyber warfare.
“They’ve taken those lessons learned there and brought them back to North Korea—that changes their capability,” Col. Ryan Donald, public affairs director for U.S.-led commands in South Korea, told reporters. “That is why the exercise looks different and over the last five years has continually evolved.”
So why Trump’s sudden policy shift? On Saturday, the U.S. commander-in-chief shared a throwback photograph posing with Kim in 2019, reiterating that the two “get along great.” The post reignited speculation that Trump is eager to stage another high-profile summit with Kim to claim a foreign policy win. Observers note a similar transactional caution in Trump stalling on a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan—the largest ever—to avoid derailing Chinese President Xi Jinping’s upcoming state visit.
But Trump’s broadside against Seoul highlights a broader global trend: partners taking steps to insulate themselves from U.S. volatility. At the same time, the Iran war has in fact turned South Korea into a major defense supplier to Gulf nations like Saudi Arabia and the UAE, which are purchasing the Cheongung-II medium-range air defense system rather than relying exclusively on American military hardware.
From Europe to the Middle East, traditional U.S. allies are replacing strategic reliance with independent insurance policies. Denmark recently opted for a Franco-Italian air defense network over the U.S. Patriot system, while Canada is re-evaluating its commitments to the F-35 program. The Dutch Central Bank migrated critical cloud infrastructure away from American tech firms to European providers to minimize systemic vulnerability.
Perhaps most remarkable was the Aug. 7 signing of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement—a NATO-style collective security pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan. After a decade of regional rivalry defined by clashes over the Muslim Brotherhood and the assassination of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, Riyadh and Ankara have found common ground amid growing questions about the extent to which they can rely on longstanding U.S. security commitments.
“It is incoherent nonsense,” says Pinkston of Trump’s flipflopping. “The credibility of the United States is under attack, and that is a direct threat to U.S. national security and international stability.”

sources.news_title: Trump Orders Major Cutback in U.S.-South Korea Military Drills, Citing North Korea Tensions
sources.text:
President Donald Trump directed War Secretary Pete Hegseth to substantially reduce the upcoming Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises with South Korea, saying the drills are expensive and send an unnecessarily hostile signal to North Korea.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
President Donald Trump ordered a significant reduction in upcoming joint military exercises between the United States and South Korea, intervening just before the allies were scheduled to begin their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield training.
Trump announced the decision Sunday in a Truth Social post, saying he had directed War Secretary Pete Hegseth to scale back the exercises because canceling them entirely at such a late stage was no longer practical.
The 11-day exercise is scheduled to begin Monday, with approximately 18,000 South Korean troops expected to participate.
Trump framed the decision around both cost and diplomacy with North Korea, arguing that continuing large-scale joint exercises works against his effort to maintain a less confrontational relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
“Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea,” Trump wrote.
He said the exercises impose significant costs, much of which he said are carried by the United States, while simultaneously projecting what he considers an unnecessarily antagonistic message toward Pyongyang.
“Therefore, and based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!” Trump wrote.
The United States and South Korea have long characterized their combined exercises as defensive training intended to maintain military readiness and ensure that American and South Korean forces can operate together effectively if a conflict occurs.
North Korea has repeatedly rejected that characterization, portraying major U.S.-South Korean exercises as preparations for an invasion.
Pyongyang issued another warning Friday ahead of this year’s Ulchi Freedom Shield, signaling that the exercises could trigger a forceful response.
Trump’s order marks another shift in the long-running military relationship surrounding the Korean Peninsula and echoes steps he took during his first administration, when some major exercises were halted or reduced while he pursued direct diplomacy with Kim.
On Sunday, Trump said North Korea had been “unthreatening and respectful” during his presidency and explicitly connected his decision on the exercises to his relationship with the North Korean leader.
The U.S.-South Korean military alliance dates to the 1953 Mutual Defense Treaty, and the two countries have conducted large-scale combined exercises for decades.
The summer training that ultimately developed into Ulchi Freedom Shield traces its roots to 1976, when South Korea’s Ulchi government mobilization exercise was combined with U.S. and allied military training.
The exercise was later known as Ulchi Focus Lens before being renamed Ulchi Freedom Guardian in 2008. It eventually evolved into the current Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise.
The allies normally conduct major combined training annually, supplemented by smaller exercises during the rest of the year.
Ulchi Freedom Shield, typically held in August, combines command-post simulations with field training and is designed to test a broad range of military capabilities.
According to U.S. Forces Korea, the exercise incorporates live, virtual, constructive and field-based training involving personnel from multiple military branches.
Training can include land, naval, air, cyber and space operations, as well as live-fire drills, logistics exercises, command-and-control operations and coordination among U.S. forces, South Korean troops and government agencies.
Last year’s exercise also included American and South Korean aircraft operating jointly through complex training scenarios.
The scale and frequency of the exercises have changed at several points when Washington sought to reduce tensions with Pyongyang.
Trump previously suspended major exercises during his first term while negotiating directly with Kim, making Sunday’s order consistent with his earlier approach of using military-training reductions as part of broader diplomatic signaling toward North Korea.
The latest decision does not eliminate Ulchi Freedom Shield. Instead, Hegseth has been directed to “substantially reduce” the exercise after Trump concluded that a complete cancellation was no longer feasible immediately before its scheduled start.
Trump also used his Sunday statement to reference a separate geopolitical issue involving Iran.
According to Trump, he recently asked South Korea’s president whether the country wanted to participate with the United States in the “Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Trump said the South Korean president responded: “No thanks!”
The comments came amid the continuing U.S. confrontation with Iran and as Trump sought to distinguish South Korea’s unwillingness to participate in that effort from his own desire to reduce tensions with North Korea.
For the Korean Peninsula, the immediate effect of Trump’s directive will be a smaller-than-planned Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise as U.S. and South Korean military officials adjust training that was scheduled to begin within hours of the president’s announcement.
Trump made clear that his decision was driven not by a rejection of the U.S.-South Korean alliance, but by his belief that the scope of the exercises is unnecessarily expensive and counterproductive to his relationship with Kim.
The order leaves the annual training in place while significantly reducing its scale, adding another diplomatic component to the administration’s approach toward North Korea at a time when Pyongyang continues to regard U.S.-South Korean military exercises as a direct threat.

President Donald Trump has ordered the Pentagon to scale back annual joint military exercises with South Korea as his war against Iran stretches the limits of U.S. aircraft carriers. Trump said South Korea wouldn’t help with his war against Iran and cited his good relationship with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
The USS George Washington is replacing the USS Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East amid growing concerns about mental health and supply issues aboard the long-deployed Lincoln. The move leaves the western Pacific without a key military asset as China shows more signs of aggression.
The BBC asked a U.S. court for help in getting documents and testimony to defend against his $10 billion defamation lawsuit. The request filed in federal court in Florida on Friday argues that Ivanka Trump, Jared Kushner and Donald Trump, Jr. have “personal knowledge” and likely have records relevant to Trump’s claims.
The Latest:
Trump blames vandals for damaged grass where he held his July 4 celebration
Trump on Sunday said vandals are to blame for large swaths of dead grass on the National Mall near the World War II Memorial — in the same spot where Trump had a stage built and hosted crowds for his July 4 celebration.
Trump made the accusation in a social media post without saying why he believes it’s the work of vandals instead of trampled turf from the Independence Day festivities. He posted a photo showing a once-grassy area by the World War II Memorial, now patchy and brown across much of the sprawling turf.
“Look what VANDALS did to the grass connecting the vandalized World War II Monument and the vandalized Reflecting Pool, which will be opened again, and better than ever, shortly,” Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
Trump has repeatedly blamed vandals for damage to his renovation projects in the nation’s capital, often without evidence and sometimes despite opposing accounts from his officials.
BBC seeks US help in getting Trump family testimony
The BBC asked a U.S. court for help in getting documents and testimony from members of Trump ’s family in connection with his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster, a court document showed.
Lawyers for the BBC argued that Ivanka Trump, Jared Kushner and Donald Trump, Jr. have “personal knowledge” and likely have records relevant to elements of Trump’s claims against the broadcaster, according to a filing Friday in federal court in Florida.
The broadcaster has been unable to serve subpoenas because the three have Secret Service protection and other security personnel around them, the filing says.
Trump filed the lawsuit in December seeking $10 billion in damages from the BBC, accusing it of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices.
The allegations center on the way a 2024 documentary edited a speech Trump gave on Jan. 6, 2021, before protesters attacked the Capitol in Washington. The lawsuit accuses the BBC of “splicing together two entirely separate parts of President Trump’s speech” to “intentionally misrepresent the meaning of what President Trump said.”
The BBC has apologized to Trump for the misleading edit, but said it had not defamed him.
US pulls last aircraft carrier from Asia as Trump turns to Iran and Americas
The USS George Washington is departing the Pacific and expected to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East amid growing concerns about mental health and supply issues aboard the long-deployed carrier. The Lincoln has had its time at sea extended from its original May return date to support operations against Iran.
The lack of a U.S. carrier in the Pacific may be short-lived if the Navy deploys another in the next couple of months. But it shows how the open-ended operations with Iran are running some American sailors ragged, analysts say, while the Trump administration further retreats from the Asia-Pacific region and focuses on the Western Hemisphere.
“The administration says that the Pacific is supposed to be the most important behind the Western Hemisphere,” said Greg Poling, director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Instead, the U.S. is “doing the exact opposite” of its previously expressed goal of pulling out of the Middle East.
Trump orders Pentagon to scale back joint exercises with South Korea
President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon on Sunday to scale back annual joint military exercises with South Korea, saying the ally declined to help with the war against Iran and citing his good relationship with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
Trump said in a social media post that the exercises, which began Monday, are not only costly but “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea, which he said “has been unthreatening and respectful” during his time in the White House.
“Therefore, and based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!” Trump wrote. The president added that he recently asked South Korea’s president if they would join the U.S. in the “denuclearization” of Iran, “and they said, ‘No thanks!’”
The move is the latest example of the president appearing to turn against an ally in favor of a leader that previous administrations have cast as an adversary.

sources.news_title: Trump scales down US-S. Korea joint military drills hours from start
sources.text:
President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military drills with South Korea, calling them “inappropriate and hostile,” just hours before exercises began Monday.
Trump cited his "good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in his latest rebuke to long-standing alliances with Western partners.
South Korean officials said the exercises had begun as planned and that they hoped the personal chemistry between Trump and Kim would bring them back to talks.
North Korea has not responded publicly, though it has previously voiced anger at the regular joint maneuvers, which take place in the South.
The drills began as American allies in East Asia fret over North Korean displays of weapons capabilities and its growing alignment with Russia as well as traditional backer China.
"Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
"These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful," he added.
He took direct aim at South Korea, writing: "I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, 'No thanks!'"
As it was too late to cancel the drills, Trump said he had ordered Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to "substantially reduce" them.
The 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises are designed to prepare for a possible war with North Korea.
Colonel Ryan Donald, spokesman for the U.S. and South Korean Combined Forces Command, has said they will simulate combat against North Korean troops steeled by their deployment on Russia's side in its invasion of Ukraine.
The maneuvers kicked off as "previously notified and scheduled", South Korea's Defense Ministry said.
Seoul's presidential office said it remained in "close coordination" with Washington over the exercises.
The office "hopes that the friendly relationship between the leaders of the United States and North Korea will lead to meaningful dialogue."
Pyongyang decries the drills as dress rehearsals for an invasion.
It recently test-fired a ballistic missile over the Sea of Japan and warned Friday it could respond to the exercises with a "new level of deterrent."
The U.S. stations about 28,500 troops in South Korea to bolster the country's defenses, a legacy of the 1950-53 Korean War that ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.
But Trump's repeated criticism of time-honored alliances has cast doubt on American commitments to security in East Asia.
Asked if China supported new dialogue between the United States and North Korea, Beijing's foreign ministry said on Monday it had "noted the relevant reports."
"Maintaining peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and promoting the political settlement of the peninsular issue are in the common interests of all parties," spokesman Lin Jian said.
In Taiwan, which relies heavily on a long-time security agreement with the United States, President Lai Ching-te said his government would propose record defense spending equivalent to over $35 billion for 2027.
China claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to annex the self-ruled island.
The U.S.-South Korean drills comprise 18,000 South Korean troops and counterparts from U.S. forces, and will focus strongly on drone warfare, GPS disruption and the role of cyberattacks, Colonel Donald had said.
Downsizing the exercise will "damage alliance coordination, slow the process of South Korea taking on greater responsibility for its own defense and weaken deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia," Leif-Eric Easley, a professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University, told AFP Pyongyang was unlikely to be moved by Trump's announcement.
"The North will only view it as meaningful if the joint exercises are canceled in their entirety rather than scaled back," he said.
Experts say North Korea has expanded its nuclear and missile capabilities since the breakdown of Trump's negotiations with Kim, whom he last met in person in 2019.
Kyiv recently said that up to 50,000 North Korean troops are due to deploy to Russia, although it has provided no evidence or a time frame for the deployment.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in making the claim, asked Seoul to supply air defense systems to protect against Russian missiles, a request that has gone unanswered by the South.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump is scaling back joint military exercises with South Korea, pointing to his relationship with Kim Jong Un and the signal the drills send North Korea.
Plus, the USS Abraham Lincoln heads home after an extended Middle East deployment, but military leaders and lawmakers disagree over whether reported problems on board have actually been addressed.
And actress Hayden Panettiere has died at just 36, after a three-decade career that began when she was a child.

Trump scales back US-South Korea drills saying exercises send ‘hostile’ signal
Joint military exercises between the U.S. and South Korea are underway, but Trump has ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the planned 10-day training mission.
Trump said South Korea declined to help denuclearize Iran and that the exercises are costly and send what he called a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea. The president also highlighted his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
It’s not yet clear what the scaled-down exercises will look like.
South Korea’s president said Monday morning the two countries have “maintained close coordination” on joint exercises and training and will continue to do so.
Trump’s order comes days after North Korea launched a ballistic missile toward the sea. Some experts said it was a test that may have been a response to planned U.S.-South Korea drills.
The scaleback has drawn criticism on Capitol Hill.
On X, Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., called it “shortsighted and a mistake,” saying North and South Korea remain technically at war and the exercises help keep U.S. forces ready to defend South Korea if the North attacks.
Eight nations condemn Israel for rejecting Trump’s peace plan ahead of Kushner’s meeting with Netanyahu
Foreign ministers from eight countries have condemned Israel’s rejection of Trump’s 15-point peace plan for Gaza. The joint statement, signed by Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan, Indonesia, Turkey, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, says Israel now bears responsibility for “obstructing the efforts to bring peace in Gaza.”
It comes ahead of a meeting Monday between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Trump’s son-in-law and Middle East envoy Jared Kushner.
Kushner met with Hamas leaders in Egypt on Sunday, discussing the group’s disarmament and the transfer of control of Gaza to a new government.
In Iran, a 60-day window for the U.S. and Tehran to negotiate a broader deal expires Monday with no agreement. The memorandum signed in June called for talks to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but those negotiations have stalled. A top official with Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said Tehran could shift from a defensive to an “offensive” posture.
Iran’s army chief is offering a $30,000 reward to anyone who kills or captures a U.S. soldier and delivers the soldier to Iranian authorities.
CENTCOM leader acknowledges USS Lincoln strain after visit
The leader of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) has weighed in on reports of poor conditions and mental health concerns aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.
After seeing it with his own eyes, Admiral Brad Cooper said the reality is more complicated.
Cooper visited the Lincoln on Saturday. The ship has been at sea for more than 200 days. During its extended deployment, it has been plagued by reports of food and supply shortages, water and plumbing problems, and deteriorating morale and mental health.
Cooper said many of the food and hot water problems were reported months ago and have since been resolved. He also said that, of the Navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, the Lincoln currently has one of the fewest mental health cases.
“This doesn’t mean that all is perfect. Find any of the nearly four million Navy veterans in America today, and they will likely tell you that service at sea for long periods isn’t for everyone,” he said.
Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., a former Marine, told ABC News’s “This Week” he’s hearing something different from families connected to the ship.
“I was just speaking to a spouse just about three days ago, and this is the current problem right now. And then it really goes to the deep, deep, deep problem here is that this administration did not plan for this war, did not plan how to get out of this war, did not really understand how this war was going to escalate. They were basically trying and hoping this war would end up just like the war in Venezuela.”
Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz.
The Lincoln has been deployed for almost nine months supporting U.S. operations against Iran. That’s more than a month beyond its original schedule.
Former Joint Chiefs Chairman Admiral Mike Mullen told ABC News he believes the government should not dismiss reports about conditions on board.
“I also believe the truth probably lies somewhere in the middle … some of these problems, I connected with Admiral Cooper last night, who was on the ship yesterday, and he had a really good visit. He told me many of these problems were early in the deployment, and they were solved. But these are morale issues on a ship, which you really have to focus on.
Mike Mullen, former joint chiefs chairman
And now, the Lincoln heads home. U.S. officials said the U.S.S. George Washington will replace it in the Middle East as part of a planned rotation.
‘Heroes’ and ‘Nashville’ star Hayden Panettiere dies at 36
Actress Hayden Panettiere has died at age 36. No cause has been announced, and her publicist said an investigation is ongoing.
Her father, Skip, described her in a statement to ABC News as “an incredible light” and “a force of nature” who brought joy to everyone around her.
She appeared on screen for over three decades, starting as a child in commercials and soap operas, with roles in “Remember the Titans” and “A Bug’s Life.” However, her breakthrough came in 2006 with “Heroes,” where she played Claire Bennet, a cheerleader with superpowers. Later, she portrayed country singer Juliette Barnes in “Nashville.”
In May, Panettiere published a memoir about her life in the spotlight and her personal struggles.
She would have turned 37 this Friday.
Beshear presses McConnell for answers as senator remains home with no return date
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear said he has yet to receive a direct response from Sen. Mitch McConnell, more than a month after first asking him to publicly comment on his health.
McConnell was hospitalized on June 14 after a fall at his Washington home, and for weeks his office released very little information about his condition. The 84-year-old later moved to a rehabilitation center and said earlier this month that he’s now back home, continuing his recovery.
Beshear first wrote to McConnell in July, asking him to update Kentuckians on his health and whether he can continue serving. He later urged McConnell to speak directly to his constituents and provide proof that he can still do the job.
“I’ve heard absolutely nothing back from Mitch McConnell,” Beshear told CBS News on Sunday.
“His bosses are the people of Kentucky. This is why the Senate, the Republican-controlled Senate, feels so broken; they feel like they’re not accountable to anyone. All he needs to do is call into this show for two minutes, or Fox News for two minutes, or do a video for two minutes to the people he’s supposed to serve. But you know what? He absolutely refuses to do it,” Beshear said.
McConnell is not running for re-election this fall. His office has released photos and written updates about his recovery, but he has not publicly stated when he plans to return to the Senate.
Four Renaissance paintings stolen from native city of Antonello da Messina
Italian police are hunting for thieves who stole four Renaissance paintings from a museum in Sicily.
The thieves targeted the museum in Messina on Saturday, when much of the city’s attention was on an annual religious procession that drew about 100,000 people. They stole three panels from the 15th-century San Gregorio polyptych, along with a small, double-sided devotional painting of the Madonna and Child.
All four are attributed to the Renaissance master Antonello da Messina — and were the only works by the artist still in his native city. The thieves took all five surviving panels but left two near a fence outside the museum as they escaped.
Police are now reviewing security footage and seeking photos from people who reported seeing suspicious activity.
Italy’s culture minister called the stolen works “extraordinary value.”

Trump Orders Military To ‘Significantly Reduce’ Joint Exercises With Longtime Ally
President Donald Trump instructed the Pentagon on Sunday evening to substantially reduce joint military exercises with South Korea. The announcement came hours before the start of the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, which began as scheduled on August 17 and is set to continue through August 27.
The exercises involve approximately 18,000 South Korean military personnel along with U.S. forces and participants from several United Nations Command member states. They include a mix of command post simulations, live field training, and other activities designed to maintain combined defense readiness. Officials had indicated the drills would address evolving capabilities, such as responses to drones, GPS disruption, and cyberattacks.
In a Truth Social post, Trump announced that the exercises will largely continue as planned this go around, but will be scaled down significantly going forward.
“Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea. These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful,” the president wrote.
“Therefore, and based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises! While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, “No thanks!” Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

No further details were immediately provided on the specific scope of the reduction, such as changes to troop numbers, types of training, or duration of particular elements. A Pentagon spokesperson referred inquiries to the White House, which did not issue additional clarification at the time.
South Korean military authorities confirmed that the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise started according to its original schedule and scale. As of August 17, officials stated that no formal request had been received from the United States to alter the planned activities, though adjustments remained possible if directed.
South Korea’s presidential office indicated it was reviewing the comments. It expressed the view that a favorable relationship between the U.S. and North Korean leaders could contribute to meaningful dialogue aimed at advancing peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula.
The office also noted ongoing consultations with the United States regarding military cooperation on other matters, including freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. South Korea’s defense ministry separately affirmed that the drills would proceed as previously notified and scheduled.
Joint military exercises between the United States and South Korea have a long history dating back decades as part of the bilateral alliance established after the Korean War. The current structure typically features two major annual combined exercises: Freedom Shield in the spring and Ulchi Freedom Shield in the summer.
During Trump’s first term, certain large-scale exercises were suspended or reduced in size following diplomatic engagements with North Korea. In more recent years, the allies have adjusted the number of field training events downward.

Trump orders Pentagon to scale back joint exercises with South Korea
Published 6:11 am Monday, August 17, 2026
President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon on Sunday to scale back annual joint military exercises with South Korea, saying the ally declined to help with the war against Iran and citing his good relationship with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
Trump said in a social media post that the exercises, which began Monday, are not only costly but “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea, which he said “has been unthreatening and respectful” during his time in the White House.
“Therefore, and based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!” Trump wrote. The president added that he recently asked South Korea’s president if they would join the U.S. in the “denuclearization” of Iran, “and they said, ‘No thanks!’”
The move is the latest example of the president appearing to turn against an ally in favor of a leader that previous administrations have cast as an adversary. Trump and others in his administration have also railed against NATO allies over perceived lack of support for his war against Iran, even as they seek to confront an increasingly aggressive Russia in the Baltic region.
It is also a sharp turnaround from how his administration has viewed South Korea in recent months.
In May, Hegseth praised the longtime ally for its “commitment to increase defense spending” and its “leadership in assuming primary responsibility for the security of the Korean Peninsula” during a meeting at the Pentagon.
“It demonstrates alliance burden-sharing that all of America’s partners would do well to follow,” the defense secretary added.
What the US military says about the joint exercises
The 11 days of exercises involving 18,000 South Korean soldiers were designed to beef up readiness against North Korean threats.
The U.S. military has said the summertime Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises reinforce “the role of the alliance as the linchpin for regional peace and security” and reaffirm “the ironclad commitment between the United States and the Republic of Korea to defend their homelands.” The exercises are one of the two main combined drills conducted by the South Korean and U.S. militaries annually, along with their springtime training.
U.S. and South Korean forces were expected to practice joint operations in complex scenarios, including a live-fire exercise to test joint precision targeting and maneuver, a wet gap crossing, and distribution of prepositioned military equipment, according to the U.S. military. South Korea’s Defense Ministry confirmed that the exercises began on Monday as planned.
The joint training started days after North Korea resumed ballistic missile testing activities in defiance of U.N. bans.
Trump’s decision was sharply criticized by Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, a former Navy pilot, who said that “hollowing out these joint exercises is shortsighted and a mistake” in a social media post made just hours after the president’s own post. Earlier this month, South Korea, the U.S. and Japan detected the launches of two ballistic missiles from North Korea in what were the North’s first ballistic weapons testing activities since late June. The missiles landed in the waters off North Korea’s east coast.
