Trump orders Pentagon to curtail military exercises with ally South Korea
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said on Sunday that he had instructed the Pentagon to reduce joint military exercises with South Korea, a longtime U.S. ally and a linchpin of America’s national security strategy in the Asia-Pacific region.
The announcement may heighten growing worries among Asian allies over what the United States is now willing to do to deter China, given the enormous distraction and resource drain of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran. The United States is running low on critical weapons and has been moving military resources out of Asia to the Middle East.
ADVERTISING
In a convoluted social media post, Trump complained that South Korea did not “join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
In the same post, he said that North Korea under Kim Jong Un had been “unthreatening and respectful” while he has been president.
In his post Trump did not mention a rift in relations in 2017, when the North Korean leader called him a “mentally deranged dotard” after Trump delivered a speech at the U.N. threatening to “totally destroy” North Korea if the United States had to defend itself or its allies.
Now Trump is speaking only of what he on Sunday called his “very good relationship” with North Korea and its leader. In his post, he said that because of those ties, he was “not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military exercises with South Korea.”
“These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful,” Trump said in his post.
Trump said that because it was too late to cancel the exercises entirely, he had asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to “substantially reduce” U.S. participation.
The U.S. and South Korean militaries have held joint exercises for more than 70 years, since 1955, after the 1953 armistice that ended the Korean War.
It was unclear just how the Pentagon would scale back its role in the joint military exercises, called Ulchi Freedom Shield, which are set to begin Monday and run for 11 days.
The exercises are held most summers with South Korea’s armed forces and with other U.S. allies in the Asia-Pacific region. North Korea has always decried the exercises as dress rehearsals for an invasion.
The exercises focus on how the allied militaries can counter a wide range of security threats, including drones and cyberattacks, while also strengthening combined defenses. They are designed to help U.S. allies defend against threats from North Korea.
The Pentagon was taken aback by Trump’s sudden announcement, according to a senior U.S. military official. Just last week, an official with U.S. and South Korean Combined Forces Command told reporters that the exercises would simulate combat against North Korean troops, who have gained crucial experience while fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine.

sources.news_title: Trump has handed a gift to Kim Jong Un and deepened concerns over US reliability
sources.text:
President Donald Trump’s sudden announcement the US is scaling back major military drills with South Korea risks renewing concerns US forces are too stretched to support crucial Western allies or maintain deterrence against autocracies that threaten them.
It’s also a gift to North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un at a time when he has ramped up his own nation’s threat to global stability –– and offered no concessions in return.
Just as the 10-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises involving tens of thousands of troops were set to begin, Trump said he had ordered the war games scaled back because North Korea has been “unthreatening and respectful” to his administration.
“These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile,” Trump posted on Truth Social over the weekend.
Trump’s statement is hard to reconcile with Kim’s actions.
The North Korean leader has significantly built up his nation’s armed forces and illegal nuclear weapons program during the past several years, even sending his soldiers to get real-world combat experience on the battlefields of Ukraine and providing Moscow with missiles that have killed Ukrainian civilians.
That help for Russia now comes with a mutual defense treaty inked two years ago with Vladimir Putin. Kim also solidified a three-way partnership with Russia and China almost a year ago in Beijing, as the three autocrats put on a very public show watching some of China’s most modern military hardware roll through Beijing in a World War II victory 80th anniversary celebration.
All the while, North Korea has been upgrading its arsenal, and Kim is frequently portrayed in state media, flanked by his teenage daughter and likely successor, overseeing military milestones –– like the activation earlier this year of a new guided-missile destroyer.
Meanwhile, in a world where the Trump administration has frequently complained about allies, especially those in Europe, not sharing in the cost of their own defense, as recently as late May it was holding up South Korea as its ideal ally.
“If you want to see what burden sharing looks like, consider the Republic of Korea. South Korea has invested consistently in its own defense, … because it does not have the luxury of treating war like an academic exercise. They live on the front lines, and so they build real combat power,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegesth said in a speech to the Shangri La Dialogue defense conference in Singapore.
Hegseth is correct. South Korea is acting out of necessity, and the Iran war has served as a reminder that the US will always move its assets to where it needs them most. The Pentagon has had to call on forces and hardware from around Asia as it has built up forces in the Persian Gulf, during a conflict that has festered for nearly half a year.
Earlier in the war, Washington moved missile interceptors from the Korean Peninsula to the Middle East. And just last week, it announced its only Western Pacific-based aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, was headed to waters near Iran to relieve the beleaguered USS Abraham Lincoln, its sister ship that has been plagued by reports of low morale after more than 200 days without a port call.
“Bilateral exercises with South Korea unnecessarily burn US resources and readiness at a time when the United States is running low on both,” said Jennifer Kavanagh, director of military analysis for Defense Priorities, a Washington, DC-based think tank that advocates for restraints on foreign policy spending.
But others take issue with her premise the exercises are unnecessary, arguing that scaling them back puts US forces –– almost 30,000 of them stationed in South Korea and over 50,000 more in nearby Japan –– in a more dangerous situation.
Trump’s move “lowers coalition readiness and puts US forces at risk with no real tangible benefit to the United States,” said retired US Navy Adm. Mark Montgomery, now a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a national security think tank based in Washington, DC.
Indeed, most of the costs for Ulchi Freedom Shield have already been incurred and whatever training is curtailed will have to be made up somewhere or US readiness will suffer, said Carl Schuster, a former director of the US Pacific Command’s Joint Intelligence Center.
Scaling back the drills and criticizing South Korea for not paying more –– something he also did in his first administration –– continues a pattern for Trump, berating longtime US allies who’ve had America’s back during the Cold War and in places like Afghanistan and the Persian Gulf, and even threatening to seize their territory, as in Greenland, part of NATO ally Denmark.
Meanwhile the US president refuses to criticize Kim, who is helping prolong Russia’s illegal war that has cost hundreds of thousands of lives in Ukraine, while using that war to refine North Korea’s arsenal, which puts nearby US troops at risk.
“What you’re seeing is the North Koreans are getting an advantage, really an unforced error on our part,” said CNN military analyst Cedric Leighton, a former US Air Force colonel.
How far Kim can now press that advantage remains to be seen.
Trump frequently changes course on a dime and as all the elements for the Ulchi Freedom drills are in place, scaling them back may not amount to much on the ground.
But North Korea has also long pursued an end to US military exercises with South Korea. On Monday it woke up to the US commander in chief saying he was ordering a drawback.
Trump, who is believed to have long coveted another meeting with Kim, may see this gesture to pave the way towards that. But his sudden about face has consequences for the US and its allies.
Few can argue that the US military can bring to bear on North Korea in 2026 what it could during Trump’s first term. When Kim tested ballistic missiles in 2017, Trump sent three US aircraft carriers to patrol the waters around the Korean Peninsula while threatening Pyongyang with “fire and fury like the world has never seen.”
Those threats would eventually get Kim to engage in three face-to-face meetings with Trump. But those meetings ultimately failed to end North Korea’s nuclear weapons program, which Kim has only grown. He’s now estimated to have dozens of nuclear warheads and has vowed to build more.
Washington’s air campaign against Iran has not seen Tehran backing down. And the only thing really falling seems to be US military readiness, as key arms stockpiles are rapidly depleted.
Scaling back the currents drills may do long-lasting damage, too, analysts warn.
Whipsawed by praise one month and criticism the next, allies may decide to leave Washington out of their long-term military planning. There’s already been a push in South Korea for Seoul to have its own nuclear weapons and not rely on Washington for deterrence.
Japan is, meantime, growing and modernizing its military at pace not seen in modern times as the post-Cold War stability ensured by the US military frays.
And multiple European nations who have stood shoulder to shoulder with the US since the Second World War are now asking real questions about whether the NATO alliance will ultimately survive Trump’s “America First” approach to global security.
That makes the world a more dangerous place, where a mistake by just one actor could ignite a regional firestorm, with a US military weakened by Iran unable to ensure American security.
“The things that we do in those exercises are critical for the joint defense not only of South Korea and Japan but also for defense of the United States as well,” Leighton said.

sources.news_title: Why Is Trump Cutting US-South Korea Military Exercises? Kim Jong Un, Iran and North Korea Explained
sources.text:
President Donald Trump instructed the Pentagon to cut significantly into the United States' involvement in joint South Korea-United States military drills, hours before the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises were set to start, on Sunday Aug. 16.
Trump referred to the expenses of the exercises, the South Korean's opposition to U.S. participation in the Iran deal, and his reported meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Trump made the announcement hours before the drills were due to get underway. Writing on Truth Social, he stated: "These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile."
Trump added: "Based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!"
The White House has not publicly detailed what specific military support it requested from Seoul in connection with Iran. Trump's post said he had recently asked South Korean President Lee Jae Myung whether South Korea would join U.S. efforts involving the "Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran," and that the response was "No thanks!"
Ulchi Freedom Shield Drills Explained
The military exercise, called Ulchi Freedom Shield, is an annual joint South Korea and U.S. military drill aimed at enhancing the defense capabilities of the two nations on the Korean Peninsula.
Since 2022, the exercise has been named Ulchi Freedom Shield. The current exercise structure is designed to include military training and government-level readiness exercises and is based on scenarios found in wartime on the peninsula, the Defense Ministry said.
The 2026 exercise began Monday, Aug. 17, and is scheduled to run through Aug. 27. Approximately 18,000 South Korean soldiers are taking part. The training also involves command-post simulations and exercises in the field, aimed at preparing the allies for changing military situations.
The U.S. military has described combined exercises with South Korea as an important part of maintaining alliance readiness. U.S. Forces Korea documents describe Ulchi Freedom Shield and Freedom Shield as major theater-level combined exercises intended to train forces for wartime missions and integrate allied and government capabilities.
South Korea Proceeds with Exercises
South Korea proceeded with Ulchi Freedom Shield as scheduled on Aug. 17 despite Trump's order.
The immediate effect of Trump's directive on U.S. participation was not clear. Reuters reported that Seoul continued to emphasize the importance of maintaining U.S.-South Korean defense coordination while the two countries carried out the scheduled exercise.
That distinction is important: Trump's announcement did not cancel Ulchi Freedom Shield. Instead, it called for a reduction in the scale of U.S. participation while the exercise was already due to begin.
Kim Jong Un Shapes Trump's Decision
Trump's decision comes in the context of his longstanding effort to maintain direct diplomacy with Kim.
Trump met Kim three times during his first presidency, including at a 2019 meeting in the Demilitarized Zone. Their diplomacy did not produce an agreement on North Korea's nuclear program, and negotiations subsequently stalled.
Trump has continued to express an interest in renewed engagement with Pyongyang during his second term. His latest comments indicate that his assessment of U.S.-South Korean military exercises is also being influenced by his stated relationship with Kim.
At the same time, North Korea continues to expand its conventional and nuclear-related military capabilities. In June, North Korean state media reported that Kim had ordered a 2.5-fold increase in ballistic and cruise missile production capacity over five years.
That creates a central tension in Trump's position: while he describes North Korea as "unthreatening and respectful," Pyongyang continues to develop and test weapons that South Korea, the United States and Japan regard as security threats.
North Korea's Recent Missile Activity
North Korea's weapons activity has continued ahead of the U.S.-South Korean drills. On Aug. 11, North Korea launched a ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the Sea of Japan, according to South Korean officials cited by Reuters. The missile flew about 700 kilometers, and the launch was described as the country's 11th suspected missile test of 2026.
The launch followed another projectile launch from Wonsan on Aug. 6. South Korea, Japan and the United States have repeatedly condemned North Korean ballistic missile launches as violations of U.N. Security Council resolutions.
North Korea has also criticized the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which Pyongyang has historically described as preparations for an invasion. The allies maintain that the exercises are intended to strengthen defensive readiness.
The timing has therefore created a competing set of signals. Trump has called for reduced exercises partly because he believes they send a hostile message to North Korea, while Pyongyang has continued missile testing and has opposed the drills.
Iran Dispute Complicates U.S.-Korea Ties
Trump's decision also reflects the changing demands placed on the U.S.-South Korean alliance as Washington conducts military operations involving Iran.
In 2026, Operation Epic Fury against Iran will be launched by the United States, the White House confirmed, revealing the campaign was a way to counterbalance Iran's nuclear and ballistic-missile capabilities.
By saying this, Trump has suggested he had hoped that South Korea would give some support to the U.S. effort. The organization, however, has not published any details of what support Seoul was requested to render or why South Korea turned it down.
South Korea's importance lies in its military alliance with Washington, which is essentially to protect the Korean peninsula. The U.S. has a significant military presence on the Korean Peninsula, with Seoul grappling with an urgent security threat from North Korea.
The Iran issue thus creates an additional wrinkle in an already complex balance of commitments in the Northeast Asia region in the context of Washington's broader military agenda.
Pentagon's Next Move Remains Unclear
The exercises are scheduled to continue through Aug. 27, but the precise elements of U.S. participation that could be reduced have not been publicly specified.
The outcome will also provide an early indication of whether Trump's latest move represents a temporary adjustment to the exercises or a broader change in the U.S.-South Korean approach to military readiness.

sources.news_title: Trump turns his back on South Korea, scales down military exercise and praises Kim
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump announced overnight between Sunday and Monday that he had decided to “significantly reduce” U.S. participation in the major joint military exercise it holds with South Korea each year, just hours before it was set to begin. In his statement, Trump specifically cited his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, and accused Seoul of failing to come to Washington’s aid when it became embroiled in the military crisis with Iran.
The joint exercise between South Korea and the U.S., which began Monday morning and is known as Ulchi Freedom Shield, is scheduled to last 11 days. It was originally planned to include 18,000 South Korean soldiers, alongside personnel from the U.S. garrison stationed in the country, which numbers 28,500 troops. The exercise is held every summer and is intended to strengthen the ability of South Korea’s armed forces and their American allies to defend against North Korea, which is armed with nuclear weapons and has recently stepped up its missile tests.
The planning for this year’s exercise took into account the experience North Korean forces have gained in the war between Russia and Ukraine, where tens of thousands of troops from Pyongyang were sent to assist Vladimir Putin’s army. U.S. military officials assess that North Korean military leaders have drawn lessons from the fighting on the Ukrainian front, and that Pyongyang’s capabilities have changed accordingly, especially regarding the use of drones, cyberattacks and GPS disruptions.
Trump’s overnight announcement reducing the U.S. role in the joint exercise, published on his Truth Social platform, joins a long list of insults the U.S. president has directed at America’s traditional allies since returning to the White House in 2025. While Trump has repeatedly called on South Korea to shoulder a greater share of defense costs, a U.S. official this year actually called Seoul “a model ally” and described it as demonstrating an impressive commitment to increasing defense spending in line with the U.S. regional strategy.
North Korea threatens and fires missile into the sea
In his overnight post, Trump attacked the exercises as “expensive,” and claimed they “send a hostile and completely inappropriate message” to North Korea — a nation that, he said, “since Donald Trump became president, is not threatening but acting respectfully.” The third-person phrasing was Trump’s own.
North Korea traditionally views the joint Washington-Seoul exercise as preparation for an invasion, and in recent days it condemned it and warned of possible retaliation and increased “deterrence” measures. As a first step, it launched a ballistic missile toward the Sea of Japan last Wednesday.
In his Truth Social post, Trump also mentioned Seoul’s refusal to take part in U.S. military actions against Iran, using it to justify reducing American involvement in the exercise. “While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, “No thanks!” Trump wrote.
On Monday morning, after Trump’s overnight statement, South Korea’s presidential office, the Blue House, said it was reviewing his post and that it “hopes the friendly relationship between the leaders of the U.S. and North Korea will lead to meaningful dialogue between the two Koreas, and to talks aimed at promoting peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula.” It also said the allies would continue close coordination on their combined defense posture and military exercises.
In response to Trump’s claim that President Lee Jae-myung had refused to join U.S. efforts to denuclearize Iran, Seoul’s presidential office said South Korea had discussed possible ways to assist militarily while considering its defense readiness on the Korean Peninsula and domestic legal procedures.
When 'Little Rocket Man' and the 'mentally deranged dotard' fell in love
It is unclear how the exercises will now be reduced, but in recent years they have shifted from live-fire drills to missile attack and cyberattack scenarios conducted through computer simulations. 
Victor Cha, head of the Korea program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, said Monday morning that by reducing the exercise, Trump may be seeking greater influence over North Korea, also against the backdrop of Pyongyang’s deep involvement in fighting alongside Russia in Ukraine. According to him, Trump may be interested in enlisting Kim to undermine ties between Moscow and North Korea, which have grown much closer in recent years.
Jenny Town, director of the 38 North program at the Stimson Center, said she believes Trump’s decision may be part of a broader effort to create a diplomatic opening with Pyongyang, something Trump has consistently wanted since returning to office, “although the random nature of this move is unlikely to impress Pyongyang very much.”
Trump mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un early in his first term as president, repeatedly calling him “Little Rocket Man” and threatening Pyongyang with “fire and fury.” Kim, for his part, boasted at the time that he would “tame the mentally deranged U.S. dotard with fire.” Later, in a surprising move before tensions escalated into military confrontation, Trump and Kim decided to hold a historic meeting in Singapore, and then met face to face two more times. 
Following the meetings and an exchange of letters between them, Trump even declared: “We fell in love.” However, those efforts did not lead to changes regarding North Korea’s determination to hold on to nuclear weapons and advance its ballistic missile program.
Trump’s overnight announcement came after he shared a photo a day earlier on Truth Social showing him with Kim Jong Un during their historic 2019 meeting, during his first term as president. “Despite the unfriendly look in this particular picture, there are many where we are smiling,” he wrote in the caption, adding: “Kim Jong Un and I get along very well!”
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said in June, during a pause in the conflict between the U.S. and Iran, that Trump now wanted to focus on resolving the North Korean issue. Lee, who is seen as taking a dovish approach toward North Korea, has moved away from the hard line of his predecessor since taking office in June 2025, and has offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions. However, North Korean authorities have so far ignored those repeated overtures.

sources.news_title: Trump Scales Back Military Exercises With South Korea Because They're Not Nice For Kim Jong Un
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Sunday that he has ordered the Pentagon to scale back the joint military exercises with South Korea that began this week.
In a Truth Social post, the president said his decision was based on his “very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” and described North Korea as “unthreatening and respectful.” He also condemned South Korea for declining to help the U.S. denuclearize Iran.
The joint exercises were expected to last 11 days and involve 18,000 South Korean soldiers, The Associated Press reported. In a statement carried by state media Friday, North Korea described the training as “a rehearsal for an aggressive war.”
Trump said that he sees the exercises as “hostile” to North Korea and costly for the U.S., but because it was too late to cancel them, he had ordered a reduction instead.
On Saturday, Trump posted a photo of himself standing next to the North Korean dictator and said the two get along well “despite the unfriendly look on this particular picture.”
It wasn’t immediately clear what scaling back the exercises would entail. South Korea’s Defense Ministry told AP that the drills had started on Monday local time as planned.
According to The New York Times, the two countries have conducted joint military exercises for over 70 years. Such exercises have been dedicated to honing the readiness of U.S. and South Korean troops so they’re prepared to respond to North Korea’s military and weapons capabilities.
Historically, North Korean leaders have criticized the exercises while finding ways to capitalize on them. Experts told The AP that North Korea has used the exercises as a “pretext” to do its own weapons testing and curry goodwill for Kim. Just last week, North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the sea ahead of the start of the drills.
It’s also not the first time that Trump has sought to curtail the exercises. He suspended the exercises in 2018 as part of denuclearization talks with North Korea, BBC News reported.
Critics of Trump’s announcement on Sunday emphasized that the move essentially aligned the U.S. president with an authoritarian leader, while undermining America’s long relationship with South Korea.
“Our ability to help defend our ally against the North Koreans is because our forces are well trained and able to coordinate with the South Koreans,” Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) wrote on X. “Hollowing out these joint exercises is shortsighted and a mistake.”

Trump said the move was influenced in part by what he described as his “very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” North Korea’s leader.
He also pointed to South Korea’s response when Washington sought support for his campaign against Iran.

sources.news_title: Trump orders cut to South Korea drills, citing ‘very good’ Kim relationship
sources.text:
President Donald Trump instructed the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” joint military exercises with long-term Asian ally South Korea, citing the cost of the drills and Seoul’s refusal to take part in actions against Iran.
Hours before exercises were scheduled to begin, Trump said on his Truth Social site he was “not happy” that the U.S. had agreed to participate and highlighted his “very good relationship” with Kim Jong Un, the leader of nuclear-armed and heavily sanctioned North Korea.
“These exercises are not only costly… but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful,” Trump wrote.
The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercises are scheduled to run until August 27, with about 18,000 South Korean military personnel participating.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff told Reuters the drills started on Monday as scheduled.
South Korea’s presidential Blue House said it was reviewing Trump’s post and “hopes that the friendly relationship between the U.S. and North Korean leaders will lead to meaningful dialogue between the two countries, opening discussions aimed at advancing peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula,” it said.
The allies would continue coordinating on their combined defense posture and military exercises, it said.
Responding to Trump’s claim that President Lee Jae Myung had refused to join U.S. efforts to denuclearise Iran, it said Seoul was discussing potential military contributions, while considering its defense readiness on the Korean Peninsula and domestic legal procedures.
A Pentagon spokesperson referred questions on the matter to the White House, which did not immediately respond to a request for details.
UP-AND-DOWN RELATIONSHIP
Trump has long sought to end or curtail military exercises with South Korea while clashing with Seoul over sharing the costs of stationing 28,500 U.S. troops in South Korea and their role in securing the broader region.
North Korea, still technically at war with the South, routinely denounces the U.S.-South Korean exercises as preparations for an invasion. Pyongyang last week fired a ballistic missile from its eastern coast towards the Sea of Japan, days after a similar North Korean short-range ballistic missile launch.
“This decision may be part of a larger effort to create a diplomatic opportunity with Pyongyang, as Trump has consistently wanted since coming back to office, although the haphazard nature of this move is unlikely to make much of an impression in Pyongyang,” Jenny Town, head of the Stimson Center think tank’s 38 North program, said in an email.
The relationship between Trump and Kim has been a roller coaster for years.
Trump once mocked the North Korean leader as “little rocket man” and threatened Pyongyang with “fire and fury,” while Kim boasted that he would “tame the mentally deranged U.S. dotard with fire.”
Yet they also took part in three summits, with Trump declaring, “we fell in love” after exchanging letters with Kim. None of these efforts led to changes in North Korea’s nuclear weapons or ballistic missile development.
Even as Trump on Sunday spoke warmly of North Korea, he pointed to South Korea’s stance on the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran.
“While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks!'” Trump wrote.
EXERCISES SHIFT TO SIMULATIONS
It’s unclear how the drills could be cut back, but in recent years, they have shifted away from live-fire exercises to computer-simulated missile and cyberattacks.
Victor Cha, head of the Korea program at Washington’s Center for Strategic and International Studies, said Trump may be seeking greater influence over North Korea as Pyongyang has been heavily engaged in support of Russia in Ukraine.
“The other way to look at this is that Trump wants to engage Kim as a way to impede the Russia-NK ties,” said Cha.
U.S. military officials have said North Korean troops, who have fought alongside Russia in its invasion of Ukraine, have gained experience from the conflict, while Ukraine said last week that North Korean-made missiles were used in a Russian ballistic missile attack on a steel plant in Zaporizhzhia.
A high-ranking U.S. Northern Command official, Lieutenant General Joseph Jarrard, last week warned that North Korea had successfully tested intercontinental ballistic missiles with “enough boost to deliver a nuclear payload anywhere in North America.”
ECONOMIC FACTORS
While Trump has repeatedly called for South Korea to shoulder a bigger burden of defense costs, a U.S. official this year called Seoul a “model ally” committed to increasing defense spending in line with U.S. regional strategy.
There are also broader economic tensions.
A former U.S. official who worked in the first Trump administration told Reuters he believed Trump is “frustrated with the intransigence” of the South Korean administration in addressing economic issues.
“The Lee government has repeatedly pursued policies antagonistic to American companies and shown little interest in following through on the historic investment deal with the United States,” the official said.
The countries signed a trade deal last year to lower Trump’s auto tariffs in exchange for Seoul’s commitment to invest $350 billion. South Korea has not announced details of its investment plan.
The allies have been at odds over a dispute involving U.S.-listed e-commerce company Coupang, which is being investigated by Seoul over a massive data leak.

sources.news_title: Trump orders Pentagon to slash military drills with South Korea
sources.text:
WASHINGTON - U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday he had ordered the Pentagon to sharply reduce joint military drills with South Korea, citing his "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Disclosing the order on social media, Trump wrote he does not like such exercises as they are "not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile" to North Korea.
Trump's comments came just before the start of the two long-standing allies' Ulchi Freedom Shield military drills and a day after he posted on Truth Social a photo of himself with Kim during the U.S. president's first term, saying he and the North Korean leader get along well.
As always, North Korea has reacted sharply to the annual exercises involving about 18,000 South Korean military personnel, about the same number as last year.
The drills, scheduled to run through Aug. 27 in South Korea and featuring both field and virtual training, are designed to bolster the countries' combined defense posture and improve alliance response capabilities against regional security threats.
This year's Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises incorporate elements of modern warfare, such as countermeasures against cyber and drone attacks, with North Korea developing its military capabilities through its support for Russia's war against Ukraine.
North Korea has long denounced U.S.-South Korea regular military drills as rehearsals for an invasion, although the two allies have described them as defensive in nature.
Last week, a spokesperson for North Korea's Foreign Ministry released a statement saying that the country will respond to "a new level of a threat with a new level of a deterrent."
In Sunday's social media post, Trump claimed that North Korea has been "unthreatening and respectful" during his presidency and he had instructed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to "substantially" scale back the latest drills, since it was too late to cancel them.
Trump also said he had recently asked South Korean President Lee Jae Myung to work with the United States on denuclearizing Iran, but South Korea had declined the request.
Trump has repeatedly said he remains open to talks with the North Korean leader. But as the U.S. war with Iran continues to drag on, he has rarely spoken about North Korea in recent months.
North Korea has long sought to be recognized as a nuclear power, while seeking the removal of economic sanctions imposed by the United States and its allies.
In 2018, Trump became the first sitting U.S. president to meet with a North Korean leader when he shook Kim's hand in Singapore. At the time, they agreed to work toward the complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula.

Trump asks Hegseth to scale back wargames with South Korea
WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon on Sunday to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea, saying it declined to help denuclearize Iran and citing his "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Trump said in a social media post that the exercises, set to start on Monday, are costly and “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea, which he said “has been unthreatening and respectful” while Trump has been in the White House.
Trump added that it was too late to cancel the drills, so he had ordered Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to “substantially reduce” them.
The president said he recently asked South Korea’s president to join the US in its efforts to denuclearize Iran, “and they said, ‘No thanks!’”
When asked about Trump’s post, South Korea’s Ministry of Defense said the military exercises would “proceed as previously notified and scheduled”.
The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield drills, scheduled to run for 11 days from August 17 to 27, will involve 18,000 South Korean soldiers. They are a regular summer fixture for South Korea’s armed forces and their US allies, designed to prepare them for defense against the nuclear-armed North Korea, which is battle-hardened from its involvement in Russia’s war on Ukraine.
North Korea on Friday threatened unspecified stern steps against the US and South Korea, describing their military drills as a “a rehearsal for an aggressive war” that are triggering greater instability in the region.
The warning was typical of the harsh rhetoric that North Korea often deploys ahead of major US-South Korean military exercises. Experts say North Korea has often used its rivals’ drills as a pretext to ramp up testing activities to expand its weapons arsenals and promote public support for the reclusive North Korean leader.
US and South Korean forces were expected to practice joint operations in complex scenarios, including a live-fire exercise to test joint precision targeting and maneuver, a wet gap crossing, and distribution of prepositioned military equipment, according to the US military.
The US military has said the summertime exercises reinforce “the role of the alliance as the linchpin for regional peace and security” and reaffirm “the ironclad commitment between the United States and the Republic of Korea to defend their homelands.”
The joint training comes days after North Korea resumed ballistic missile testing activities that are banned by the UN.
Earlier this month, South Korea, the US and Japan detected the launch of a short-range ballistic missile from North Korea in what was the North’s first ballistic weapons testing activity since late June. The missile landed in the waters off North Korea’s east coast.
North Korea has been pushing hard to enlarge its nuclear and missile arsenals since Kim’s high-stakes diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019. Experts say Kim likely believes a bigger weapons arsenal would increase his chances for wresting more concessions from the US in future negotiations.
Trump met with the North Korean leader three times during his first term to discuss the country’s nuclear program, most recently in 2019. Since returning to office, Trump has expressed interest in continuing those discussions.
Trump’s announcement came a day after he posted a photo of himself standing next to North Korea’s Kim, writing that the two leaders get along great “despite the unfriendly look on this particular picture.”
This is not the first time that Trump has sought to end the exercises. During his first term he also issued a surprise announcement that called the wargames “provocative.”
“We will be stopping the wargames, which will save us a tremendous amount of money, unless and until we see the future negotiation is not going along like it should,” Trump told reporters after his 2018 meeting with Kim in Singapore.

Costly Drills and a Public Rebuke for Seoul
The American and South Korean defence chiefs confirmed plans last week to stage their annual 11‑day Ulchi Freedom Shield command post exercise.

Diplomats are now examining why the White House chose to connect security arrangements on the Korean peninsula with cooperation on Iran.
Missile Tests and Stalled Nuclear Talks
The presidential directive comes after a series of military developments in the region. Earlier this month, Pyongyang conducted ballistic missile tests that violate United Nations sanctions, with South Korea, the United States and Japan detecting a second launch within days of the first.

Allied military commanders had presented this year's joint training as a response to emerging global security concerns, including North Korea sending troops to support Russia's war in Ukraine.

North Korea's foreign ministry criticised the planned drills on Friday, issuing a statement rejecting foreign threats and saying the regime would exercise its sovereign right to self‑defence.

President Donald Trump has said the US will “substantially reduce” joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his “very good relationship” with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un.
He also noted on Truth Social that South Korea had recently declined to join the US in the “denuclearisation” of Iran.
“These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile,” Trump posted.
Seoul said the drills with the US would proceed “as scheduled”. Pyongyang has not yet commented. It comes after North Korea this month conducted ballistic missile tests banned by the United Nations.
Trump said in his social media post on Sunday that it was “too late to cancel”, as the US and South Korea were due to start their annual military exercises on Monday.
He added: “While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks!’”
Trump’s announcement came less than 24 hours after he posted an old photograph of himself and Kim from 2019, writing the two were great friends “despite the unfriendly look on this particular picture”.
Last week, US and South Korean military leaders held a joint press conference announcing Ulchi Freedom Shield.
They said the 11-day event would be similar in scale to previous years, with about 18,000 South Korean soldiers participating.
During the news conference, military leaders also mentioned North Korea’s deployment of troops to aid Russia’s war against Ukraine.
US military spokesperson Ryan Donald said “our training accounts for that threat”, referring to North Korean soldiers returning from the battlefield. About 28,500 American military personnel are stationed in South Korea.
On Friday, North Korea’s foreign ministry condemned the joint military drills as “a rehearsal for an aggressive war”.
The joint exercises come days after South Korea, the US and Japan detected the second North Korean missile test in days.
Pyongyang has accelerated efforts to expand its nuclear and missile programmes since the collapse in 2019 of Kim’s high-profile diplomacy with Trump during his first term in the White House.
He became the first ever sitting US president to set foot in North Korea when he visited seven years ago.
For Seoul, Trump’s post is a mixed message. On the one hand, they have been requesting Trump engage with Pyongyang and the post raises hope that he might bring Kim back to the table.
But Trump is also hinting that he is unhappy with South Korea’s unwillingness to make direct military or logistical contributions to the US hostilities with Iran.
He has also expressed displeasure with other allies for their hesitance to get involved in the conflict, including Japan, France and the UK.
Trump’s move to downsize joint military exercises with South Korea is not without precedent.
He suspended the exercises entirely in 2018, during denuclearisation negotiations with Kim. He said at the time that the annual drills were “provocative” towards North Korea and stopping the “war games” would save the US “tremendous amount of money.”
The exercises were again scaled back in 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Last week, South Korea’s president proposed talks with its northern neighbour on officially ending the war between the two that is technically still active since an armistice was signed in 1953.
Trump has noted multiple times in the past that the US is providing security to South Korea without getting much in return.
He has criticised the number of troops it has stationed in the peninsula and the money spent.
This has complicated Washington’s relationship with Seoul, which sees the troops as core to its alliance with the US.
Seoul has tried to defuse the tension earlier this year, committing $350bn to investing in the US. And last year President Lee Jae Myung described Trump as a peacemaker. – BBC
